new_statements.quote: Tone has morphological significance in the language. Passive nominals are derived from their gerundive counter parts by changing the tonal pattern from High-Low to Low –Low.
new_statements.citation: Mahider (Mahder) Tesfu. 2003. Morphology of Malo. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University. Section 1.7.5 (6) 'Tone', p. 17 (p. 29).
new_statements.locator: ch. 1, sec. 1.7 'The phonology', subsec. 1.7.5 Morphophonemic processes, item 6 'Tone', printed p. 17 (examples (19) on p. 18); pp. 29-30
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (147 pp., text present; extracted text, no scanned). p. 29 carries printed page number 17 and item "6. Tone" under 1.7.5 Morphophonemic processes; the passage reads exactly "Tone has morphological significance in the language. Passive nominals are derived from their gerundive counter parts by changing the tonal pattern from High-Low to Low –Low." (line break after "from" only). Examples (19) gaco/gaco, pito/pito follow on printed p. 18 (p. 30) with no visible tone marks; the key (p. v) lists "high tone" / "low tone" entries whose diacritic glyphs are blank in the PDF. The same statement recurs at 2.2.2.6 Passive nominals (p. 42, "Tone has grammatical significance in Malo..", examples…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only primary description treats Malo as having tone with a morphological function (gerundive HL vs. passive nominal LL); it never mentions stress or accent, and its only other suprasegmentals are gemination and vowel length (sec. 1.7.2). Azeb Amha's 2007 Encyclopaedia Aethiopica entry (based on this thesis plus one interview) adds that a tone/accent difference between short subject and possessive pronouns 'probably exists' but is undescribed. No statement of where word stress falls exists in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the thesis's tone diacritics (key p. v: high tone / low tone) did not print in the PDF (empty boxes), so even the HL/LL examples gaco 'cutting' vs gaco 'piece left after cutting', pito 'sweeping' vs pito 'dirt left after sweeping' carry no visible marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (derived nominals). Azeb Amha 2007 (EAE 3: 710): 'there probably exists a tone/accent difference between the two (this question is not discussed in Mahider Tesfu 2003; the author's own data are insufficient to draw a conclusion)' -- i.e., prosody is essentially undescribed. Family context (Hirut Woldemariam 2004: 25): Ometo varieties with descriptions (Wolaitta, Zayse, Gamo, Haro) are tone-accent languages with one high tone per simple word; no such statement has been made for Malo.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Melo' = Ethnologue 'Melo' = the language its speakers and the linguistic literature call Malo / Malittso (Malo-Koza woreda, Gamo Gofa). All sources examined use 'Malo'; same variety, no dialect split reported.
